exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: A printable workshop workbook with exercises, worked answers, and a closing action.
exampleAnswers.Working context: This fictional sixty-minute workshop helps a small team describe one project clearly. The HTML reveals worked answers after each exercise; the PDF includes them for facilitator review.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Exercise: Name the user · Time: 10 minutes · Output: One concrete audience
Exercise: Describe the task · Time: 15 minutes · Output: One observable action
Exercise: Set the boundary · Time: 15 minutes · Output: Included and excluded work
Exercise: Choose the check · Time: 10 minutes · Output: Acceptance evidence
Exercise: Close · Time: 10 minutes · Output: Owner and next step
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
Exercise: name the task: Start with “A visitor needs to…” and finish with something observable. Worked answer: “A visitor needs to find today’s opening hours on a phone.” This is easier to test than “make the site engaging.”
Exercise: set a boundary: List the smallest useful result and one tempting addition to exclude. Worked answer: publish the menu and location; keep online ordering outside the first release.
Exercise: choose the check: Describe how another person will verify the result. Worked answer: ask a reader to find the hours and menu, record where they hesitate, and revise the unclear path.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: workbook layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching portrait document PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
